title: The Story That Wasn't Finished: Two Writers Talk

dialogue.speaker: Leila
dialogue.text: Have you finished your narrative writing assignment? I've been struggling with it all week.

dialogue.speaker: Marcus
dialogue.text: Not yet. I wrote three different openings and deleted them all. The problem is I keep starting with too much background information.

dialogue.speaker: Leila
dialogue.text: Same! I spent two pages describing the setting before anything even happened. My teacher said the reader was "waiting for the story to start."

dialogue.speaker: Marcus
dialogue.text: That's exactly the feedback I got too. She said: "Jump in. The reader doesn't need to know everything before the first action."

dialogue.speaker: Leila
dialogue.text: So what did you do? Did you rewrite it?

dialogue.speaker: Marcus
dialogue.text: I started in the middle of the action — in medias res, you know? The opening line is now: "The door was already open when she arrived." That sets up the past continuous and the main action at the same time.

dialogue.speaker: Leila
dialogue.text: Oh, I like that. It immediately creates a question: why was the door open? The reader wants to know.

dialogue.speaker: Marcus
dialogue.text: Exactly. And then I used the past perfect to fill in the backstory — what had happened before she got there. But only in small pieces, not all at once.

dialogue.speaker: Leila
dialogue.text: That's what I've been trying to do. But my problem is tense consistency. I keep slipping into the present tense by accident.

dialogue.speaker: Marcus
dialogue.text: I had that problem too. My teacher told me to read each paragraph aloud. If something sounds wrong, it usually is. Our ear knows the language better than our eye sometimes.

dialogue.speaker: Leila
dialogue.text: That's a good tip. What about dialogue? I find it hard to integrate conversations without losing the narrative flow.

dialogue.speaker: Marcus
dialogue.text: I keep dialogue short and purposeful. Each line should reveal character or move the plot. If it doesn't do one of those, it shouldn't be there.

dialogue.speaker: Leila
dialogue.text: That's strict! But probably right. What's your story actually about?

dialogue.speaker: Marcus
dialogue.text: It's about a woman who returns to her childhood home after twenty years. She's looking for something — but what she finds is not what she expected.

dialogue.speaker: Leila
dialogue.text: That sounds really interesting. The classic return narrative — but with a twist. I'd read that.

dialogue.speaker: Marcus
dialogue.text: I hope it works. The hardest part is the ending. I don't know whether to leave it open or resolve it clearly.

dialogue.speaker: Leila
dialogue.text: I think that depends on what the story is about at its core. If it's about ambiguity and uncertainty, leave it open. If it's about finding something, close it.

dialogue.speaker: Marcus
dialogue.text: You know, that's actually really helpful. I think it's about uncertainty. So maybe the door at the end should be open again.

keyPhrases.context: Starting a narrative in the middle of events
Keeping the same tense throughout a narrative
Advance what happens in the story
The smooth movement of the story without interruption
A story about going back to somewhere or someone from the past

vocab.definition: beginning a story in the middle of the action, rather than at the beginning
vocab.example: "The door was already open when she arrived." — starting in medias res.

vocab.definition: using the same narrative tense throughout without unintentional shifts
vocab.example: Tense consistency is broken when a past tense narrative slips into present tense.

vocab.definition: the sequence of events in a story
vocab.example: "Each line should reveal character or move the plot."
